BNS is the current criminal code in force from 1 July 2024 and contains offences against women and children in Chapter V, including rape, sexual harassment, voyeurism, stalking and related offences.

BNSS is the current criminal procedure code in force from 1 July 2024 and replaced the CrPC for criminal procedure.

The Domestic Violence Act protects an aggrieved woman in a domestic relationship from domestic violence and provides civil relief through protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation orders.

The POSH Act provides a workplace complaint and redressal framework through Internal Committees and Local Committees as provided by the Act.

POCSO protects every child below 18 years from sexual offences and establishes child-sensitive reporting, investigation and trial procedures.

The Dowry Prohibition Act prohibits giving, taking and demanding dowry, with separate statutory provisions for different offences.

The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act addresses offences relating to trafficking and exploitation connected with prostitution and provides statutory police and protective mechanisms.

The MTP Act, as amended, regulates lawful medical termination of pregnancy and includes privacy protection for women.

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 declares talaq covered by the Act void and illegal and provides related rights and consequences.

The Maternity Benefit Act provides statutory maternity benefits for eligible women in covered establishments, with important amendments made in 2017.

Rape is defined in BNS Section 63, while punishment is provided in Sections 64 and 65 depending on the applicable clause and facts.

BNS Section 74 addresses assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty.

BNS Section 75 addresses sexual harassment and contains different punishments for different acts listed in the section.

BNS Section 77 addresses voyeurism.

BNS Section 78 addresses stalking.

BNS Section 80 addresses dowry death.

BNS Sections 85 and 86 address cruelty by a husband or relatives of a husband and define cruelty.

PWDVA Section 31 addresses breach of a protection order by the respondent.

POCSO Sections 3, 5, 7, 11 and 19 address different child sexual offences and mandatory reporting.

Information relating to a cognizable offence is governed by the current BNSS procedure.

Medical examination in sexual-offence cases is governed by the current BNSS procedure and related law.

A magistrate can grant protection, residence, custody, monetary and compensation-related relief under the Domestic Violence Act.

Emergency support numbers should be treated as rapidly changing service information and verified against official government directories.

One-Stop Centres provide integrated support such as medical, legal, counselling, police liaison and temporary shelter.

Women affected by violence can seek free legal aid through the legal-services system.

A woman can seek free legal aid through NALSA and the appropriate State, District or Taluk Legal Services Authority.

The official India Code text lists Sections 63–90 in Chapter V as current offences relating to women and child.

Individual sections should be used for precise legal answers rather than treating Sections 63–78 as one combined provision.

The BNSS governs current criminal procedure, including FIR and complaint procedure, investigation, medical examination procedure and trial-related safeguards.

Specific rights should be answered using the relevant BNSS section.

Sections 2 and 3 define relevant terms and domestic violence.

Sections 18–23 provide protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders, compensation orders and interim or ex parte orders.

Section 31 separately addresses breach of a protection order.

The Act provides for constitution of an Internal Committee under Section 4 and a Local Committee under Section 6, and Section 9 governs the complaint process.

The earlier dataset's universal '90 days' statement is not retained as a blanket rule because different statutory timelines apply to different stages.

The Act includes penetrative sexual assault, aggravated forms, sexual assault, sexual harassment and mandatory reporting provisions.

Child-friendly procedures and Special Courts are governed by the statutory framework and should be answered using the relevant sections.

Section 3 addresses the penalty for giving or taking dowry, and Section 4 addresses the penalty for demanding dowry.

The exact punishment should be read from the current statutory text rather than summarized as a single uniform penalty.

Sections 3–6 address offences such as brothel-related conduct, living on earnings of prostitution, procuring and detaining persons.

Sections 16 onward provide rescue and protective procedures, while later provisions address protective homes and related processes.

Section 3 governs when pregnancies may be terminated by registered medical practitioners, and Section 5A protects the privacy of a woman.

Claims about eligibility up to specific gestational limits should be read together with the amended Act and current rules.

The Act includes Section 3 on talaq being void and illegal, Section 4 on punishment, Section 5 on subsistence allowance, Section 6 on custody of minor children and Section 7 on the procedural character of the offence.

The Act contains eligibility and benefit provisions, and the 2017 amendment expanded maternity benefit in specified circumstances.

The dataset should answer eligibility and duration using the current statutory text and applicable conditions rather than one blanket entitlement.

Section 63 defines rape.

Sections 64 and 65 provide punishments that vary by the statutory circumstances, including aggravated situations and the age of the victim.

The dataset should not reduce these provisions to a single universal punishment.

Section 74 is a current criminal-law provision under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

The statutory punishment should be read from the current section text rather than summarized as a single oversimplified maximum.

Section 75 distinguishes among categories of conduct.

The applicable punishment depends on the clause and facts, so the dataset should preserve that distinction instead of using one blanket sentence.

Section 77 addresses voyeurism.

Punishment differs between a first conviction and a subsequent conviction under the statutory text, so the dataset records the provision without collapsing it into one penalty.

Section 78 addresses stalking, including the conduct described in the statutory provision.

Punishment differs between a first conviction and a subsequent conviction, so the current law should be read as written.

Section 80 is the current BNS provision on dowry death.

The punishment is governed by the statutory section and should not be summarized as a single unsupported phrase.

Section 85 creates the offence of cruelty by a husband or relative of a husband, while Section 86 defines cruelty for this purpose.

They should be read together.

Section 31 provides the penalty for breach of a protection order.

The record should distinguish the civil protection remedies under the Act from the separate criminal consequence for breach.

These sections cover distinct offences and reporting obligations.

Penalties vary by the offence and aggravated circumstances, so they should not be represented as one uniform punishment.

The current criminal procedure is under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

The previous CrPC wording should not be presented as current law.

The dataset therefore retains a general current-law statement and marks detailed timing claims for review unless verified against the BNSS text.

The source states that every district has a District Legal Services Authority and that victims of violence are a priority group for free legal aid.

Section 144 is the current criminal-procedure maintenance provision.

It applies when a person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain an eligible wife, child or parent under the statutory conditions, and the Magistrate may order a monthly allowance.

Official Mission Shakti material describes Sambal for safety/security and Samarthya for empowerment.

Sambal includes One Stop Centres, Women Helplines, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and Nari Adalats; Samarthya includes support components such as Shakti Sadans, Sakhi Niwas, PMMVY, Palna and empowerment hubs.

112 is the Pan-India single emergency response number for emergencies requiring police, fire, health or other coordinated emergency assistance. It is an emergency facility and should be used for genuine emergencies.
The official Mission Shakti directory is the authoritative source to verify the current routing and availability of Women Helpline 181. This dataset therefore treats it as a periodically verified support contact rather than a permanent statutory provision.
The official child helpline source states that 1098 operates under Mission Vatsalya in coordination with State and District functionaries and is integrated with ERSS-112 for children in crisis.
The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal states that online financial fraud can be reported through helpline 1930. This support record should not be used as a substitute for other cybercrime reporting procedures.
NALSA's official women assistance page states that women can seek free legal assistance through Legal Services Authorities and can call the toll-free helpline 15100 for guidance. Women are eligible for free legal aid under the legal services framework.
Mission Shakti and One Stop Centre documentation describe integrated support services for women affected by violence, with coordination across medical, police, legal, counselling and temporary shelter services according to the programme framework.
Central laws generally apply across India, but implementation and support services may differ by State or Union Territory. The model should ask for the state or UT instead of inventing local contacts or schemes.
